opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that the research itself was bad. It was a mismatch between what I was doing day to day and what I actually cared about.

When I first arrived at Stanford I was in the EE department, and the project I joined was quite close to the hardware and signal side of things. It was very rigorous work, and I learned a lot about doing things carefully. But after a while I noticed that I wasn't excited when I woke up in the morning. The questions felt very well-defined and incremental: you optimize a component, you improve a metric by a bit. I kept asking myself, even if this works perfectly, how does it change the way machines understand or act in the world?

What really pulled at me was a more fundamental question: how can an intelligent system perceive the 3D world, understand objects, and eventually interact with them? At that time, around 2016 and 2017, deep learning was taking off, and computer vision and graphics were changing very fast. I would go to talks in the CS department and come out feeling much more energized than I did in my own lab. That was a very clear signal.

There was also a personality fit issue. I like problems that are a bit open-ended, where you have to define the problem yourself before you solve it. In my early EE work the problem was largely given to me. Eventually I made the decision to move toward 3D vision and geometry, and that's how I ended up working with Leo Guibas. Looking back, it was a risky switch, since I gave up some time and familiarity, but it was the right call. Research is a long game, and if you don't feel genuine curiosity about the problem, it's very hard to persist through all the failures.

fable-5.1.text:
When I first arrived at Stanford, I was placed in a group that was doing fairly traditional electrical engineering work. It was a lot of signal processing and hardware-oriented problems. The research was rigorous and the people were excellent, but I quickly realized that the questions themselves didn't excite me.

What I cared about was more fundamental. I wanted to understand how machines could perceive and reason about the physical world, how a system could look at a scene and actually understand what it was seeing. The projects I was assigned felt like they were optimizing one more component in a pipeline whose overall direction was already decided. I would finish a task and feel that even if I succeeded perfectly, the result wouldn't change how anyone thought about anything.

There was also a cultural mismatch. In that environment, progress was measured in incremental improvements on well-defined benchmarks. I was more drawn to problems where the formulation itself was still open, where you had to decide what the right question even was. That kind of ambiguity made some of my colleagues uncomfortable, but it was exactly what energized me.

So after about a year, I started spending more and more time with the computer vision and graphics people, and eventually I moved over. In hindsight, that first year wasn't wasted. The mathematical training and the discipline about experimental rigor stayed with me. But I learned something important about myself, which is that I need to believe the problem matters in a deep way before I can do good work on it.
